perspective:
Mason’s accessible information is limited to what he personally experienced, observed, was told, inferred, felt, or did:

- He works as an accountant at a small community center and interacts with Martha Moua professionally as a colleague; they are not personally close.
- He reviewed financial reports and noticed discrepancies: healthcare expenses appeared unusually high compared with usual spending.
- Based on those discrepancies, he initially suspected Martha might be mismanaging funds and felt suspicious and anxious.
- He initiated a discussion with Martha, telling her the numbers did not add up and pointing to the healthcare expenses.
- He heard Martha say there may have been a misentry and that she would review and correct any errors.
- After reviewing/clarifying with Martha, he learned the discrepancies were a simple clerical error, not mismanagement.
- He felt relieved but embarrassed about his initial suspicion, apologized to Martha, and heard her accept the apology, say errors happen, and suggest double-checking entries next time.
- He came to believe Martha was competent and that the real problem was inadequate financial management systems. He felt frustrated with the system but empathetic toward Martha.
- He proposed creating a new, more robust financial system. He said he would draft a proposal and wanted Martha’s input. He heard Martha agree and offer to help address identified gaps.
- He drafted a proposal, believed it would benefit operations, and was uncertain whether management would approve or implement it.
- He told Martha about the proposal and his uncertainty. He heard her call it solid, encourage confidence, and agree to help gather data. He planned a detailed presentation and asked for her help.
- He presented the proposal to management.
- After presenting, he felt satisfied with his efforts but physically and mentally exhausted, believing he had done everything possible and that the decision was now up to management.
- He told Martha he thought the presentation went well. He heard Martha praise him and suggest taking time off.
- He thanked Martha, said he would take a few days off to recharge and reflect, and hoped for good news. He heard Martha wish him a good break and offer help while away.
- His own actions include reviewing reports, discussing discrepancies with Martha, apologizing, proposing/drafting the new system, preparing and presenting the proposal, and planning/taking time off.

He does not have access to Martha’s private thoughts or motivations, management’s internal deliberations, or any events he did not observe or hear about directly.
